blog_digest.title: How much risk should we take?
blog_digest.topic: position sizing; risk target; Kelly
key_rules: Position exposure = (1/N) x C x (T/V) x (F/10): C capital, T risk target (annualised stdev), V instrument risk (annualised stdev), F forecast with average absolute value 10 on a -20..+20 scale, N expected number of concurrent positions
Rule of thumb: annualised stdev is roughly 14 x daily ATR

Risk target = the most conservative of four limits: personal loss tolerance, broker leverage cap, 'safe leverage' limit (max leverage = tolerable loss / worst plausible one-day crash), and half-Kelly (target = half the expected Sharpe ratio)
Suggested starting target for a single-rule, single-instrument system: 12%; professional managers typically 10-30%; his own live target is 25%
numbers: Half-Kelly: expected SR 0.5 implies a 25% risk target
Safe-leverage example: 23% one-day crash and 50% tolerable loss gives max leverage 2.17; with 15% instrument risk that caps the target at 32.6%
Worked example of the four limits: tolerance 25%, broker 50%, safe-leverage 32.6%, Kelly 12% -> chosen target 12%
Sharpe benchmarks quoted: average retail trader -1.0; simple single-indicator mechanical system 0.24; diversified systematic retail trader about 1.0; top hedge funds 2-4
blog_digest.reasoning: Size is proportional to capital and target risk and inversely proportional to instrument risk, so volatile instruments get smaller positions and total risk stays near target. Forecast strength scales exposure linearly. Kelly logic ties the affordable risk target to the true edge, and because the edge is uncertain and full Kelly is too aggressive, half-Kelly is the practical cap.
caveats: Stdev is an imperfect risk measure; fat-tail crashes (e.g. 1987) can exceed what it implies
Sharpe figures are illustrative benchmarks, not measured for a specific strategy

Reader comments: a 25-day vol lookback can give huge positions after quiet spells; author says his own system uses a vol floor and a forecast-based V matched to holding period, and prefers simple over log returns
blog_digest.quote: The better your trading system is, the more risk you can take.

blog_digest.title: How fast should we trade?
blog_digest.topic: costs; speed limit; trading speed
key_rules: Total annual cost = holding (roll) cost + trading cost x number of trades; express costs in Sharpe-ratio units by dividing by annualised instrument stdev
Speed limit: spend no more than one third of expected pre-cost SR on costs
Max trades per year = ((expected SR / 3) - holding cost) / cost per trade
Small trader with market orders pays about half the spread; he reports about a quarter of the spread with a simple execution algo
Keep at least three trading-rule variations for diversification but drop the fastest ones that breach the speed limit
numbers: Eurodollar example: execution cost 0.0058 SR per trade, roll cost 0.026 SR per year; with expected SR 0.24 the cost budget is 0.08, giving max about 9.3 trades per year
Stop distance (fraction of annual vol) maps to trades per year: 0.3 -> 11.9, 0.4 -> 7.8, 0.5 -> 5.4
EWMAC 64,256 averages SR about 0.28 and trades about 1.1 times a year; the Law of Active Management would predict SR 1.68 for EWMAC 2,8 but actual is about 0.07
Net of Eurodollar costs the fastest rules lose money; EWMAC 8 only just passes the limit
If costs rise 50% when volume doubles, speeding up stops helping around EWMAC 16
blog_digest.reasoning: Costs grow roughly linearly with the number of trades whereas the gross edge from trading faster grows more slowly (at best like the square root of trade count, by the Law of Active Management, which is an upper bound). Net return therefore peaks at some speed, and the one-third cost budget is a heuristic to locate it.
caveats: Law of Active Management is an idealised upper bound that fast rules usually miss
Cost assumptions are snapshot values (COVID-era spreads were wide); very fast trading changes costs via market impact
Comparing average pre-cost SR across instruments against Eurodollar costs is a deliberate simplification
Smoothing and buffering change turnover and should be tested in the backtest
blog_digest.quote: SPEED LIMIT: DO NOT SPEND MORE THAN ONE THIRD OF YOUR EXPECTED PRE-COST RETURNS ON COSTS

blog_digest.title: Should I run my trading system at a fixed expected volatility target?
blog_digest.topic: vol targeting; forecast strength and realised risk
key_rules: Baseline: expected risk = target risk x relative aggregate forecast strength x relative correlation factor (RCF); i.e. portfolio risk is deliberately allowed to float with aggregate forecast strength
Fixed-risk variant: multiply all positions by target / ex-ante portfolio risk; forecast-adjusted variant multiplies by (forecast strength x target / ex-ante risk), which reduces to 1/RCF
Aggregate forecast strength = instrument-weighted sum of absolute forecasts divided by the average absolute forecast (10)
Risk multiplier capped at 3.0
numbers: Sharpe: original 0.93; fixed-risk 0.64; forecast-adjusted (remove only RCF) 0.87
Aggregate forecast strength varied from below 0.2 to above 1.3 once all 20 instruments were in (about sixfold)
Fixed-risk made skew more negative at daily/weekly/monthly horizons and worsened the 1% daily tail, though kurtosis improved
blog_digest.reasoning: Aggregate forecast strength predicts future risk-adjusted returns (ex-post returns slope upward with it), so forcing constant risk throws that information away and cuts Sharpe. The RCF varies with current positions and correlations without any link to expected return, so removing only that term keeps most of the performance.
caveats: Skew and kurtosis estimates carry large sampling error
Scaling positions by a constant ignores the extra trading each variant would cause, so costs are approximate
Correlations break down in crises so realised risk can still exceed expected
Author would not implement the forecast-adjusted version in his own system because of complexity and no clear gain
blog_digest.quote: it throws away the information provided by aggregate forecast strength

blog_digest.title: Do non-binary forecasts work?
blog_digest.topic: forecast scaling and capping; linearity of forecast response
key_rules: Forecast = calibrated estimate of future risk-adjusted return, scaled to average absolute value 10; cap at +/-20 (twice the target average)
Holding period = 256 / annual turnover (EWMAC 16,64 on Eurodollar is about 17 business days)
Normalised return = N-day price change divided by daily vol x sqrt(N)
Test design: bucket forecasts by sign and quantile (bin size 2 gives four buckets) and t-test adjacent buckets for positive slope, plus first versus last bucket
Decided not to add an intercept to correct the long bias in returns, since that would add a parameter and a built-in long bias
numbers: Eurodollar, uncapped, sign only: mean normalised return 0.21 for positive forecasts vs 0.02 for negative (t = 7.6); positive forecasts about 2x as frequent
Pooled over all instruments, capped, four buckets: adjacent-bucket t-stats 10.4, 13.5, 16.0; first-to-last t-stat 35.7
Every EWMAC variant (2_8, 4_16, 8_32, 32_128, 64_256) passed pooled; ewmac2_8 weakest at about t = 3.6
Carry pooled first-to-last t-stat about 40.9
On Eurodollar alone the segment t-stats were marginal (1.8-4.2); 8 instruments in the dataset would fail the test for this rule
blog_digest.reasoning: Stronger forecasts are followed by larger risk-adjusted returns across the whole range, so scaling position size with forecast strength (non-binary) is supported over binary +/-1 positions. At the extremes uncapped returns flatten or revert (trend exhaustion; very quiet markets giving huge forecasts and then reversing), which capping largely neutralises.
caveats: Eurodollar was chosen to illustrate interesting behaviour; strong results come from pooling
Without capping, slow rules show reversion in the tails
Non-linear response functions invite overfitting; non-binary sizing needs more capital
Digest note (not from the post): overlapping N-day returns are autocorrelated so the p-values are probably overstated
blog_digest.quote: the stronger your forecast, the larger your position should be.

blog_digest.title: Forecast linearity and forecasting mean reverting volatility
blog_digest.topic: volatility estimation; vol mean reversion; forecast scaling
key_rules: Risk-adjusted forecast = expected return / recent vol, with recent vol an exponentially weighted estimate of roughly one-month half-life

Blended vol forecast = (1 - p) x current vol + p x slow vol, where slow vol = long-run average of vol (EWM span 2500 days, about 10 years); eyeballed p about 0.33, regression gave about 0.98 x current + 0.41 x (slow - current)
Untested proposal: double slow-momentum forecasts then cap at 10 (instead of 20) to avoid the tail reversion
numbers: Test rule ewmac64_256 pooled: at extreme forecasts realised vol ran 10-20% above the current-vol forecast, overstating expected risk-adjusted returns by a similar amount
Blended vol cut the uncapped vol error to under 5% and removed about two-thirds of the bias
Vol-forecast R-squared on S&P 500: 0.884 blended vs 0.84 for current vol alone
blog_digest.reasoning: Large forecasts mostly occur when recent vol is unusually low; low vol tends to revert upward, often just as the trend turns, so realised vol exceeds the forecast and realised risk-adjusted returns fall short. Blending in long-run vol removes most of that bias; the remainder is attributed to trend exhaustion.
caveats: Motivating chart used one market (S&P 500)
Blend weight fitted in-sample (author argues it is stable)
Regression residuals have heavy autocorrelation (Durbin-Watson about 0.03) and fat tails so fit statistics are fragile
Did not test whether better vol forecasts actually raise returns; warns of overfitting a non-linear fix
blog_digest.quote: trends tend to get exhausted after a while, so a very strong trend is due a reversal.

blog_digest.title: My trading system (as of December 2021)
blog_digest.topic: full system spec: rules, forecast weights, IDM, instrument selection, dynamic optimisation
key_rules: Rule families: EWMAC at 4,8,16,32,64; assettrend and normmom at 2-64; breakout 10-320; relative momentum 10-80; acceleration 16,32,64; carry spans 10,30,60,125; relative carry; skew (abs and relative, 180 and 365); slow mean reversion in asset class (mrinasset160); mean reversion in the wings (mrwrings4)

Handcrafted forecast weights: trendy group 0.6 / other 0.4. Within trendy: assettrend 0.15, relmomentum 0.12, breakout 0.12, momentum 0.10, normmom 0.11. Within other: carry 0.18, relcarry 0.08, accel 0.06, skew 0.04, mean reversion 0.04
Asset-class weights: equity 0.22, bonds and STIR 0.19, ags 0.15, FX 0.13, metals and crypto 0.13, oil/gas 0.13, vol 0.05
IDM set at 2.5, deliberately below the estimated value
Vol estimate = 70% recent vol + 30% ten-year average vol; momentum-style forecasts attenuated when vol is above its historic level
Cost filter: skip an instrument for a rule if cost exceeds 0.01 SR per trade (speed limit); instruments sampled for spreads before inclusion
Positions set by dynamic optimisation (minimum tracking error to the unrounded optimal portfolio, integer contracts) plus buffering
numbers: 146 instruments, 109 with positive Sharpe, median Sharpe 0.27, average correlation of subsystem returns 0.05
Equal-weighted rule Sharpes: carry 0.90-0.95; momentum64 0.73; normmom32 0.82; mrwrings4 -0.94; mrinasset160 -0.63
Backtest (daily): Sharpe 1.31, mean 30.1%, stdev 23.0%, Sortino 1.81, Calmar 0.70; monthly Sharpe 1.14; hit rate 62.6%
blog_digest.reasoning: Trend following is the core and carry is the single most valuable rule. Mean-reversion rules lose money alone but are strongly negatively correlated with trend rules so handcrafting still gives them a small weight because backtest Sharpes are uncertain. Vol attenuation addresses the observed deterioration of momentum when vol is high.
caveats: Backtest is heavily in-sample and calibrated, so overstates achievable performance
Live weights are manual whereas backtests use automated handcrafting
Rule Sharpes are crude averages across instruments
Risk target, forecast cap and EWMAC scalars are not stated in the post
blog_digest.quote: the biggest change to my system this year has been the introduction of a dynamic optimisation system

blog_digest.title: Portfolio construction through handcrafting: The method
blog_digest.topic: handcrafting; diversification multiplier; portfolio weights
key_rules: Start from equal weights; for assets with different risk use inverse-volatility weights (weight proportional to 1/sigma, normalised) and convert to cash weights by dividing by sigma and renormalising; skip this step for trading strategies that already target a common risk
Group assets hierarchically: equal vol weights across groups, then within groups, multiplying weights down the tree
Diversification multiplier for a group = group risk / single-asset risk; multiply the group's raw weight by it and renormalise
Risk targeting with leverage: scale by target risk / natural risk of the portfolio. Without leverage: if target < natural risk hold cash = (natural - target)/natural
Original method matched correlations to seven candidate matrices (0, 0.5, 0.9) and applied conditional Sharpe multipliers; he later replaced both (see B09, B10)
numbers: S&P 500 (16% vol) and US 2y bonds (2% vol): inverse-vol cash weights 11.1% / 88.9%; natural portfolio risk 2.5-3.5%
10% target at correlation 0.5 needs leverage about 3.2; with no leverage 59.8% S&P / 40.1% cash-bonds
DM example: A,B correlated 0.5 with C uncorrelated, equal vol 10%: DM of group AB 1.155, final weights 26.8% A, 26.8% B, 46.4% C
Correlation estimate uncertainty with 100 observations: 95% interval -0.2 to +0.2 for rho = 0 and 0.34 to 0.63 for rho = 0.5
blog_digest.reasoning: Standard deviations are the most stable estimates so inverse-vol is a sound base. Grouping stops a cluster of similar assets taking most of the risk budget just because it has many members, and the diversification multiplier gives correlated groups more capital because their combined risk is lower than the raw weight implies.
caveats: Assumes equal Sharpe ratios unless conditioned; designed for long-only weights
Candidate-matrix and Sharpe-adjustment steps superseded by the author's later posts
Human vs machine groupings can differ
blog_digest.quote: Equal weights should be the starting point for any portfolio allocation.

blog_digest.title: Fit forecast weights by instrument, by group, or pool everything; or a blend?
blog_digest.topic: fitting forecast weights; pooling; overfitting; cost speed limit
key_rules: Compare weights fitted per instrument, per k-means cluster of instruments (4 clusters), pooled over all instruments (gross returns pooled, costs per instrument), and a simple average (blend) of the three
Speed limit: zero a rule for an instrument if its cost exceeds 0.13 SR
Test universe 14 instruments, 12 rules (EWMAC 4/16 and 64/256, carry, breakouts, mean reversion, relative momentum, assettrend, normmom, relcarry, skew, kurtosis) not cherry-picked for profitability
numbers: Net Sharpe (all rules / with speed limit): individual 0.602 / 0.545; groups 0.656 / 0.546; everything 0.651 / 0.587; blend 0.656 / 0.587; equal weights 0.657 / 0.726
Cost drag in SR (all rules / with limit): individual 0.120 / 0.083; groups 0.109 / 0.085; everything 0.096 / 0.079; blend 0.090 / 0.083; equal weights 0.178 / 0.074
blog_digest.reasoning: Per-instrument fitting uses little data and gives noisy weights; pooling brings more data and more robust weights, and grouping similar instruments also groups similar cost levels. Averaging fitting schemes usually improves out-of-sample behaviour. Differences between schemes are small and equal weights are competitive.
caveats: Sharpe differences are small; one 14-instrument subset, one rule set, one period
Four clusters is arbitrary
Equal weights winning with the speed limit would not hold for a less curated rule set
Speed limit lowers net Sharpe for most schemes, so its benefit is mixed
blog_digest.quote: Having said that a clearly stupid thing to do is to fit weights for each instrument individually

blog_digest.title: Optimising my way out of a small fund (part five): dynamic optimisation with greedy algo (Mr Greedy, part one)
blog_digest.topic: dynamic optimisation; instrument selection for small accounts
key_rules: Objective: minimise the stdev of the tracking-error portfolio (current integer positions minus unrounded optimal positions) using the instrument covariance matrix, plus trading costs
Cost penalty = per-instrument cost x abs trade size x a shadow-cost multiplier (default 10 in this version)
Greedy search: start at zero, each step add or remove one contract in the direction of the sign of the optimal position, take the single best improving step, repeat until none improves
Constraints supported: reduce-only, do-not-trade, min and max positions
numbers: 45 instruments, $100K: Sharpe unrounded 1.17, rounded 1.06, optimised 1.19; costs about 0.13 SR in all cases
Return correlation with the unrounded portfolio: optimised 0.94, rounded 0.97
Held 6 positions on average out of 45 (max 18)
At $50K: optimised Sharpe about 0.1 above rounded but about 0.2 below unrounded
blog_digest.reasoning: Many near-equivalent integer portfolios exist, and minimising tracking-error variance gives a more stable target than maximising utility. A greedy one-directional search is usually good enough and scales far better than grid search; risk of untradeable markets is substituted into correlated tradeable ones.
caveats: Author later said the method did not work as well as hoped: his cost calculations were wrong for sparse positions and turnover was understated (see B13 for the corrected version)
Greedy search can stop at local optima
In-sample backtest with fixed shadow cost
blog_digest.quote: It didn't work, at least not as well as I'd hoped.

blog_digest.title: Optimising my way out of a small fund (part six): greedy algo part two
blog_digest.topic: dynamic optimisation; buffering; costs; turnover
key_rules: Shadow cost raised to 250, reasoned from an assumed Sharpe of 1.0 (not grid-searched)

Portfolio-level buffer using tracking error as utility: if tracking error between current and unrounded optimal positions is below the buffer, do nothing; otherwise optimise, then trade only the share (x - b)/x of the required trades, where x is current-vs-optimised tracking error and b the buffer
Buffer size 0.0125 (1.25% annualised risk), i.e. 10% of a 25% average risk target
Costs measured in dollars per historic trade, deflated by changes in price vol; roll costs assume rolling the pre-roll position
Shrink the correlation matrix to keep it positive semi-definite
numbers: Dynamic 114-instrument portfolio, $500K: gross SR 1.336, net 1.287, cost about 5bp SR per year, turnover 51 times a year, return correlation with unrounded portfolio 0.986, holds a quarter to a third of instruments
Static 34-instrument benchmark: gross SR 1.322, net 1.275, turnover 37.5 times a year
Unrounded 114-instrument portfolio SR 1.359, so the integer constraint costs only a few bp of SR
blog_digest.reasoning: The greedy algorithm always takes the sign of the optimal position, so every sign flip forces a trade regardless of shadow cost, which sets a turnover floor. A portfolio-level buffer that trades only the excess tracking error over the buffer fixes that and replaces instrument-by-instrument buffering.
caveats: Author states the previous post's results were wrong, mainly from understated turnover and costs
Shadow cost and buffer come from assumptions, not formal calibration
Forecast weights fitted in-sample; benchmark depends on the chosen 34 instruments; static backtest has under 15 instruments before 2000
No clean general fix for non-PSD pandas correlation matrices beyond shrinkage
blog_digest.quote: every time the underlying forecast changes sign, we'll definitely trade regardless of the size of the shadow cost.

blog_digest.title: An exogenous risk overlay
blog_digest.date: 2020 (about May; exact date not shown in the fetched text)
blog_digest.topic: risk management; position scaling in crises
key_rules: Overlay gives a multiplier between 0 and 1 applied to all positions; it is the minimum of three components
Maximum expected risk: min(1, 2 x target risk / current expected risk)
Correlation risk: set all correlations to 1 (absolute weights): min(1, 4 x target / expected risk under that matrix)
Stdev risk: replace each instrument's vol with its 99th percentile estimate over about 10 years (2,500-day rolling quantile): min(1, 6 x target / expected risk under those vols)
Inputs: 30-day EWMA stdev, 120-day EWMA correlation; config keys max_risk_fraction_normal_risk 2.0, _correlation_risk 4.0, _stdev_risk 6.0
numbers: Backtest realised risk 23.7% against 25% target; 6-month rolling risk ranged from about 10% to above 40%
Overlay cut annual return and risk by roughly 3% each; Sharpe about 0.94 with vs 0.956 without (text is ambiguous which is which)
Slightly less positive skew, lower kurtosis, better 1% quantile, slightly shallower drawdowns
blog_digest.reasoning: The core system's inverse-vol scaling and Kelly-style sizing assume roughly Gaussian returns with predictable vol and correlation. When correlations or vols spike against open positions, expected risk can jump far above target; the overlay caps exposure in those states without touching the signals.
caveats: Thresholds 2, 4, 6 are calibrated choices not derived theory; warns against tuning them for performance (overfitting)
Core risk model is Gaussian; some large outliers remain unpredicted (possibly bad data)
Backtest on a subset of instruments with price data still being cleaned
blog_digest.quote: The vast bulk of the risk management load is being carried by the core system.

blog_digest.title: How much should we get paid for skew risk? Not as much as you think!
blog_digest.topic: skew; geometric return; leverage and Kelly
key_rules: Choose leverage to maximise geometric return at a chosen point of the outcome distribution: the median (full Kelly) or the 10% quantile (conservative)

Build returns by mixing Gaussians to get series with the same Sharpe but different skew and left-tail fatness, bootstrap at each leverage level, and read the price of skew off indifference curves of equal geometric mean
numbers: Kelly investor: going from skew -3 to +3 is worth at most about 4bp of SR; 10%-quantile investor at most a couple of bp
Left-tail fatness worth at most about 5bp (Kelly) or 3bp (10% investor)
Kelly optimal leverage rises from about 2.7 to 3.7 (lowest SR) or 4.2 to 5.6 (highest SR) going from most negative to most positive skew
Headline: about 6bp of SR per 5 units of skew at best, so a 0.5 skew difference should cost under 1bp; the market price implied by a 0.30 SR drop is roughly 50x too high
blog_digest.reasoning: Skew mainly bites when leverage is high because a fat left tail is punished by compounding; conservative investors who use less leverage are barely affected. Sharpe ratio drives most of the geometric return, so skew is second order and should earn only a small premium.
caveats: Brute-force bootstrapping gives noisy clouds, some non-monotonic curves
Assumes freely available leverage; interaction of leverage with the Kelly point not fully analysed
Depends on chosen quantile and bootstrapped returns; blog exploration not peer-reviewed
Negatively skewed strategies can still be dangerous with leverage
blog_digest.quote: Sure, get it if it's free, but don't pay much for it otherwise.

blog_digest.title: Kelly versus Classical portfolio theory, and the two kinds of uncertainty premium
blog_digest.topic: Kelly; leverage; Sharpe uncertainty
key_rules: Kelly: optimal leverage f* = r/s^2 and optimal risk target s* = r/s (r arithmetic expected excess return, s unlevered stdev, risk-free zero)
Utilitarian: risk target = maximum risk tolerance s_max; proposed compromise s* = min(r/s, s_max)
SR sampling variance approx (1 + 0.5 SR^2)/N (Lo 2002) under i.i.d.; use a conservative percentile of the SR distribution to set leverage (uncertainty appetite)
numbers: SR 0.5, 10 years monthly data (N = 120): median optimal risk 50% and leverage 5; half-Kelly 2.5
Confidence that leverage is not too high -> risk target: 10% -> 9.2%; 25% -> about 17%; 50% -> 50%; 75% confidence (25th percentile) -> SR about 0.29, risk 29%, leverage 2.9
Half-Kelly corresponds to roughly 22% confidence in this example
Case SR 0.2 long-only: Kelly target 20% (leverage 2); case SR 1.0 equity-neutral: full Kelly 100% risk (leverage 20) versus practical 15% risk appetite
blog_digest.reasoning: Kelly leverage depends on the true Sharpe ratio which is poorly estimated, so size using a conservative point in its sampling distribution. Greater uncertainty aversion lowers the risk target, so an external risk-appetite cap rarely binds; uncertainty aversion and risk aversion are hard to separate in practice.
caveats: Stdev treated as known; Gaussian i.i.d. returns assumed (no skew, autocorrelation, instability)
Uncertainty-appetite framework is the author's own proposal not established theory
Commenters objected that a single vol figure ignores SR; author replied that short-term leverage risk dominates
blog_digest.quote: Frankly this is a bit of a cop-out by the Kelly people

blog_digest.title: Dynamic trend following
blog_digest.topic: trend rules; vol-scaled positions; dynamic stops; skew trade-off
key_rules: Base: EWMAC 16/64 binary forecast with stop gap 0.5 x annualised stdev (X-factor 8 on daily vol)
Dynamic vol control: position = (initial vol / current vol) x initial position, with stop gap scaling with current vol
Dynamic stop: X-factor 2 when vol-normalised P&L <= 0, rising linearly to 8 at P&L of 8, capped at 8; cutoffs chosen by eye from Eurodollar
numbers: Instrument-level gross Sharpe: neither 0.19; dynamic vol 0.25; dynamic stop 0.05; both 0.07
blog_digest.reasoning: Vol scaling shrinks positions in high vol, which trims exposure to big trending winners, lowering skew but raising Sharpe. Dynamic stops cut losers fast and lift trade skew but close positions early and sharply lower Sharpe. The effects roughly offset when combined, a no-free-lunch trade-off.
caveats: Gross of costs (buffering would curb the extra trading from vol scaling)
Stop parameters not optimised, tuned by eye on one instrument
Trade-level and return-level skew differ a lot, so conclusions depend on measurement frequency
blog_digest.quote: the market does not know what my position is or has been, or how much profit I've made.

blog_digest.title: Vol targeting: a CAgR race
blog_digest.topic: vol targeting vs fixed-size trend following; compounding and skew
key_rules: Compare fixed-size one-entry-one-stop (1E1S), fixed-size reverse-on-signal (1E1E), binary vol-targeted with buffering (BV) and continuous-forecast vol-targeted with buffering (FV, 20% stdev target) on about 100 futures, EWMAC 8,32 / 16,64 / 32,128 / 64,256 and an equal-weighted combination, at the CAGR-maximising leverage rather than equal Sharpe
No fitting
numbers: At leverage 1 (combined EWMAC): CAGR FV 25.8%, BV 19.7%, 1E1E 19.3%, 1E1S 11.3%; Sharpe FV 1.18, BV 1.15, 1E1S and 1E1E 0.88; monthly skew FV 1.41, BV 0.78, 1E1S 1.98
CAGR-optimal leverage is about 5x (FV), 7x (BV), 6x (1E1S), 3x (1E1E), implying 60-120% annualised vol, not practical
Slow rule EWMAC512 CAGR: FV 7.1%, BV 8.2%, 1E1S 3.6%, 1E1E -1.4%
blog_digest.reasoning: CAGR depends on mean and variance; positive skew helps and negative skew hurts compounding at high leverage. Vol targeting's Sharpe advantage outweighs its modest skew disadvantage across sensible risk levels, and only reverses at extreme leverage.
caveats: Backtests with assumed costs (costs would need to be about 8x higher to reverse the result)
Depends on author's rules and instruments
Skew is unstable, especially for 1E1E; slow rules have few independent observations
At 6x leverage 1E1S has a 100%+ loss day (ruin risk)

blog_digest.title: Should we trade momentum differently when vol changes?
blog_digest.topic: forecast attenuation by volatility regime; trend rule performance
key_rules: Normalised vol = current EW daily % vol (about one month) divided by its own 10-year (2,500-day) rolling mean, lagged one day; regimes by backward-looking quantiles (bottom 25% low, middle 50% medium, top 25% high)
Attenuate forecasts by multiplier L = 2 - 1.5Q, Q = vol percentile (0 to 1), smoothed with 10-day EWMA, forecasts capped at +/-20
Applied to EWMAC 2_8 to 64_256 and carry
numbers: In high vol, fast momentum underperforms slow more than usual and returns of all rules fall; Medium vs High difference p about 0.00 for every EWMAC, carry p = 0.32
With a 3-day lag the Medium-vs-High p-values rise to about 0.01-0.14 (Low-vs-High stays 0.00)
blog_digest.reasoning: Momentum and carry degrade when vol is high, more so for faster rules. The pattern persists without costs so it is not just a cost story. No mechanism was established; commenters suggested vol mean reversion whipsawing fast systems.
caveats: Regime cutoffs and smoothing chosen by judgement
Effect weakens with a realistic 3-day lag; gains modest and not significant for 64_256 and carry
t-tests treat pooled daily observations as independent despite overlap and autocorrelation
Backtest of author's own data, motivated by the 2020 crisis
blog_digest.quote: To return to the original question: yes we should change our trading behaviour as vol changes.

blog_digest.title: Is the degradation of trend following a cohort, instrument or environment effect?
blog_digest.topic: trend decay
key_rules: Group instruments by data start decade; compare rolling 5y average SR per cohort, EWMAC 2,8 to 64,256 and carry, pre-cost
numbers: Strategy nine non-compounded return >500% in 1970s, >200% each next three decades, average return roughly halved since 2010
1972 start with 11 instruments; ~100 instruments in test list
1991 cohort 7 instruments
blog_digest.reasoning: No cohort effect (old instruments not better); weak instrument decay in 1991 cohort; decline across all speeds looks environmental, so restricting to older/newer instruments cannot fix it. Carry shows slightly more instrument decay.
caveats: Pre-cost
Small cohorts
Pre-1990 cost adjustment uncertain; fast trend may never have worked as well as backtests suggested
blog_digest.quote: Overall though, this does look an enviroment effect with noise.

blog_digest.title: Scream if you want to go faster (costs vs optimal momentum speed)
blog_digest.topic: trading speed / costs
key_rules: Slow down as instruments get more expensive: pre-cost optimal speed is flat across costs
Speed limit: annual cost (turnover x SR cost per trade) <= 0.13 SR units
Cost ceiling ~0.007-0.01 SR units per trade to trade at all
numbers: 160 instruments, EWMAC2-64
Turnover approx EWMAC2 42, 4 20, 8 9, 16 3.8, 32 2.3, 64 2.1
All six rules need cost <0.00283; EWMAC64 alone <0.021
Optimal speed net ~3.5 cheapest vs ~5 costliest (scale 1-6)
